overview: Buganda developed around the Kabaka and institutions connecting royal authority, chiefs and clans. Its palace architecture and musical traditions remain important expressions of Baganda identity in Uganda.

items.text: Kasubi’s royal complex uses timber, reeds and thatch at monumental scale. The palace built in 1882 became a royal burial place in 1884.
The tomb ensemble includes barkcloth-wrapped poles and a drum house. Its buildings and rituals preserve living knowledge through maintenance and rebuilding.
The Lukiiko developed from councils advising the Kabaka. Its structure changed during the nineteenth century and again under the 1900 Buganda Agreement.
Recorded royal repertoires feature drums, xylophones, lyres, flutes and harps. Twentieth-century recordings and later performances document musicians passing skills between generations.
The royal institution was abolished in 1967 and restored in 1993. Its continuing cultural role should not be confused with uninterrupted political sovereignty.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi
